course.title: Chess Mastery: From Beginner to Intermediate
course.description: A comprehensive 25-part course taking you from absolute beginner to a solid intermediate chess player. Covers piece movement, basic tactics, opening principles, middlegame strategy, endgame fundamentals, pattern recognition, calculation training, and practical tournament preparation.

blocks.value: Welcome to the 64-Square Battlefield

Chess is played on an **8×8 square board** with alternating light and dark squares. The board is positioned so that each player has a **light-colored square on their right-hand corner** (the mnemonic: 'white on right'). Understanding the board's geometry is essential because every piece's power depends on its relationship to these squares.

blocks.alt: Standard chessboard setup from White's perspective
blocks.caption: The starting position: White pieces on ranks 1-2, Black on ranks 7-8.

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: 2D chessboard diagram — Standard orientation with White at the bottom. Coordinates (a1-h8) visible on all four sides. Pieces in starting position: White pawns on rank 2, rooks on a1/h1, knights on b1/g1, bishops on c1/f1, queen on d1 (white square), king on e1. Black mirrors this on ranks 7-8. Clean, flat design with Merida-style pieces. Light squares in cream (#F0D9B5), dark squares in brown (#B58863).
How Each Piece Moves
Each of the six piece types moves in a unique pattern. Master these movements before anything else — they are the alphabet of chess language.
The King

The **King** moves **one square in any direction** — horizontally, vertically, or diagonally. It is the most important piece (the game ends when the king is checkmated), but also one of the weakest in terms of mobility. The king may never move into check (a square attacked by an opponent's piece).
The Queen

The **Queen** combines the powers of the **rook and bishop**. She moves any number of squares horizontally, vertically, or diagonally. The queen is the most powerful piece on the board (worth approximately 9 pawns), but remember: she cannot jump over other pieces.
The Rook

The **Rook** moves any number of squares **horizontally or vertically**. Like the queen, it cannot jump over pieces. Rooks are particularly powerful when they work together on open files (columns with no pawns) or when they reach the **7th rank** (for White) or **2nd rank** (for Black).
The Bishop

The **Bishop** moves any number of squares **diagonally**. Each bishop is confined to one color — the light-squared bishop never leaves light squares, and the dark-squared bishop never leaves dark squares. This is why having **both bishops** (the 'bishop pair') is often an advantage — they control squares of both colors.
The Knight

The **Knight** has the most unique movement: it moves in an **'L' shape** — two squares in one direction and then one square perpendicular, or one square in one direction and then two squares perpendicular. The knight is the **only piece that can jump over other pieces** (friend or foe). This makes it especially valuable in closed positions where other pieces are blocked.

blocks.alt: Knight movement showing all 8 possible squares from center
blocks.caption: A knight on d5 can jump to 8 squares: b4, b6, c3, c7, e3, e7, f4, f6.

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: 2D chessboard diagram — Knight placed on d5 (center of board). All 8 possible destination squares highlighted with green dots. Arrows showing L-shaped paths. Other pieces on the board to demonstrate jumping ability. Coordinates visible. Clean diagram style with subtle drop shadows on pieces.
The Pawn

The **Pawn** is the most complex piece despite its simple appearance. It moves **forward one square** (never backward or sideways). On its **first move**, a pawn may advance **one OR two squares**. Pawns capture **diagonally forward one square**. The pawn's special moves — **en passant**, **promotion**, and its ability to block paths — make it strategically profound despite being the weakest piece (worth 1 point).

blocks.question: Which piece can jump over other pieces?
blocks.explanation: The Knight is the only piece that can jump over other pieces. This unique ability makes it especially powerful in crowded positions.

blocks.question: How many squares can a knight reach from the center of the board (e.g., d5)?
blocks.explanation: A knight in the center of the board (like d5) can reach 8 squares. From the edge it reaches fewer (4-6), and from the corner only 2. This demonstrates the principle: pieces are generally more powerful in the center.

blocks.question: Select all pieces that can move diagonally:
blocks.explanation: King, Queen, Bishop, and Pawn (when capturing) can all move diagonally. The Rook moves only horizontally/vertically, and the Knight moves in an L-shape.

blocks.question: What is the standard FEN string for the starting position of a chess game?
blocks.explanation: This FEN (Forsyth-Edwards Notation) describes the starting position: lowercase for Black, uppercase for White, numbers for empty squares, 'w' for White to move, 'KQkq' for castling rights, '-' for no en passant target.

parts.partTitle: Part 2: Special Rules — Castling, En Passant & Promotion

blocks.value: The Three Special Moves of Chess

Beyond standard piece movement, chess has three special rules that fundamentally shape strategy: **castling** (king safety + rook activation), **en passant** (a special pawn capture), and **promotion** (transforming a pawn). Understanding when and why to use these moves separates beginners from developing players.
Castling: The Only Double Move

**Castling** is the only move where two pieces move: the **king moves two squares toward a rook**, and the **rook jumps over the king** to the adjacent square. There are two types: **kingside castling** (O-O, shorter distance) and **queenside castling** (O-O-O, longer distance but often more active rook).

**Conditions for castling:**
1. **Neither the king nor the rook may have moved** previously in the game
2. **No pieces between the king and rook**
3. **The king may not be in check** at the start of the move
4. **The king may not pass through check** (the square it crosses must not be attacked)
5. **The king may not end up in check**

blocks.caption: Kingside castling (O-O): King moves from e1 to g1, rook from h1 to f1.

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Side-by-side 2D chessboard diagrams — Left panel shows 'Before': White king on e1, rook on h1, pieces cleared between them. Right panel shows 'After': king on g1, rook on f1. Arrows indicating movement paths. Red X marks on squares the king cannot pass through if attacked. Coordinates visible. Clean split-screen comparison style.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 a6 4.Ba4 Nf6 5.O-O
blocks.output: Position after 5.O-O — White has castled kingside. King safely tucked on g1, rook active on f1. Black has not yet castled. Evaluation: slight advantage to White (+0.3) due to better king safety.

blocks.value: En Passant: The 'In Passing' Capture

**En passant** (French for 'in passing') is a special pawn capture. If a pawn moves **two squares forward** from its starting position and lands **beside an enemy pawn**, that enemy pawn has the option to capture it **as if it had moved only one square**. This capture must be done **immediately** on the next move — the opportunity is lost after that.
This rule exists to prevent a pawn from bypassing capture by moving two squares. It was added to chess in the 15th century when the two-square pawn advance was introduced.

blocks.caption: After 1...d5, White can play 2.exd6 e.p., capturing the d5 pawn as if it moved to d6.

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: 2D chessboard diagram sequence — Three panels showing progression. Panel 1: White pawn on e5, Black pawn on d7. Panel 2: Black plays ...d7-d5 (two squares), landing beside White pawn. Panel 3: White captures exd6 e.p., removing Black pawn from d5 and placing White pawn on d6. Arrows showing the two-square move and the diagonal capture. 'e.p.' label clearly visible.
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 c6 3.dxc6 e.p.?
blocks.output: Illegal! After 2.exd5, Black played ...c6 (one square). Since the c-pawn did NOT move two squares from its starting position, en passant is NOT available. White must make a different move.

blocks.value: Promotion: A Pawn's Reward

When a pawn reaches the **opposite end of the board** (8th rank for White, 1st rank for Black), it must be **promoted** to a queen, rook, bishop, or knight. Nearly always, players choose a **queen** (called 'queening'), as it is the most powerful piece. Choosing a different piece is called 'underpromotion' and is rare but sometimes necessary for specific tactical reasons (e.g., avoiding stalemate).

blocks.output: Position after 1.h8=Q+ — White pawn promotes to queen with check. Black king on h1 is now in check from the new queen on h8. White wins easily.

blocks.caption: Left: Promoting to queen (h8=Q). Right: Rare underpromotion to knight (h8=N#) for checkmate.

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Side-by-side 2D chessboard diagrams — Left panel: White pawn on h7, Black king on h1. After h8=Q, queen on h8 delivers check along the h-file. Right panel: Different position where h8=Q would be stalemate, but h8=N delivers checkmate. Arrows showing check lines. 'Q' and 'N' promotion labels. Clean instructional style with color-coded check indicators (red glow around checked king).

blocks.question: Under what condition is castling illegal?
options: A piece stands between king and rook
blocks.explanation: All listed conditions prevent castling. Additionally, the king cannot pass through check or end in check. Even if the rook has moved but the king hasn't, kingside/queenside castling on that side is impossible.

blocks.question: How many moves does a player have to capture en passant after the opponent's two-square pawn advance?
blocks.explanation: En passant must be played immediately on the very next move. If you don't capture right away, the opportunity is permanently lost.

blocks.question: Select all pieces a pawn CANNOT promote to:
blocks.explanation: A pawn cannot promote to a king (you can only have one king) or to another pawn (that would defeat the purpose of promotion). It can promote to queen, rook, bishop, or knight.

blocks.question: What is the algebraic notation for queenside castling?
blocks.explanation: Kingside castling is written as O-O (two capital O's), while queenside castling is O-O-O (three capital O's). These are letter O's, not zeros.

blocks.value: The Object of the Game

The ultimate goal of chess is to **checkmate** your opponent's king. But to understand checkmate, you must first understand **check** (when the king is under attack) and **stalemate** (a special drawing condition). These three concepts form the tactical and strategic foundation of every chess game.
Check: The King is Under Attack

A **check** occurs when the king is under attack by one or more enemy pieces. When your king is in check, **you MUST get out of check immediately**. You have exactly three ways to escape:

1. **Move the king** to a safe square
2. **Capture the attacking piece**
3. **Block the attack** (only works for line pieces — queen, rook, bishop — not knights or pawns)
A move that leaves your king in check is **illegal**. You cannot 'pass' on responding to check. The game cannot end in check — if no escape exists, it is checkmate.

blocks.caption: Three legal responses to check: moving the king, capturing the attacker, or blocking the line of attack.

Panel 2: 'Capture' — White knight on f3 captures checking queen on d4 (red X on queen, arrow showing capture). Panel 3: 'Block' — White bishop moves to e3 to block queen's diagonal attack on e1 (arrow showing bishop movement, blue line showing blocked attack). Each panel has descriptive label. Coordinates visible.

blocks.value: Checkmate: The Game Ends

**Checkmate** occurs when the king is in check and there is **no legal way to escape**. The game ends immediately — the checkmated player loses. Checkmate is the only way to win a chess game (other than resignation or time forfeit).
The **Fool's Mate** is the fastest possible checkmate: **1.f3 e5 2.g4 Qh4#**. White's weakened kingside allows Black's queen to deliver checkmate on move 2. The '#' symbol denotes checkmate.

blocks.caption: Fool's Mate: The fastest checkmate in chess, achieved in just 2 moves by Black.

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: 2D chessboard diagram — Final position of Fool's Mate. Black queen on h4 delivering checkmate to White king on e1. White pawns on f3 and g4 shown as weaknesses. Red glow around White king indicating checkmate. Arrows showing queen's attack lines (diagonal to e1, horizontal along 4th rank). Move list: 1.f3 e5 2.g4 Qh4#. Annotation '#'. Clean diagram with subtle checkmate visual effect (red border around board).

blocks.output: Checkmate! Black wins. The White king on e1 cannot: (1) move to d1, d2, e2, or f2 (all controlled by queen), (2) capture the queen (protected by king), or (3) block (queen is adjacent). Game over in 2 moves.

blocks.value: Stalemate: A Tragic Draw

**Stalemate** occurs when a player has **no legal moves** but their **king is NOT in check**. Unlike checkmate, stalemate is a **draw** — neither player wins. This makes stalemate a powerful defensive resource for the losing side and a dangerous trap for the winning side.
Beginners often accidentally stalemate when they have a winning position. The key rule: **if the king is not in check and cannot move, AND no other piece can move, it is stalemate**.

blocks.alt: Stalemate position: Black to move, no legal moves, king not in check
blocks.caption: Stalemate! Black has no legal moves, but the king is not in check. The game is a draw.

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: 2D chessboard diagram — Black king on h8 corner. White queen on g6, White king on g8. Black king's only escape squares: h7 (controlled by queen), g8 (occupied by White king, also controlled), g7 (controlled by queen). No Black pieces left to move. Yellow highlight around Black king indicating stalemate (not check). Blue '½-½' draw symbol. Annotation text: 'Stalemate — Draw!'

blocks.output: Stalemate position — Black to move. King on h8 has no legal squares (all controlled by queen or opponent king). No other Black pieces exist. Result: ½-½ Draw. White should have played Qg7+ or Qh6+ to force checkmate instead.

blocks.value: Other Drawing Conditions

Beyond stalemate, chess has several other drawing conditions:

• **Insufficient material:** Neither side can checkmate (e.g., king vs. king, king + knight vs. king)
• **Threefold repetition:** The same position occurs three times with the same player to move and same castling/en passant rights
• **50-move rule:** 50 consecutive moves by both players without a pawn move or capture
• **Mutual agreement:** Both players agree to a draw

blocks.question: What is the fastest possible checkmate in chess (Fool's Mate)?
blocks.explanation: Fool's Mate is achieved in 2 moves: 1.f3 e5 2.g4 Qh4#. It requires White to make two weakening pawn moves that open the kingside.

blocks.question: In a stalemate position, is the king in check?
blocks.explanation: By definition, stalemate occurs when the king is NOT in check but the player has no legal moves. If the king were in check with no escape, it would be checkmate, not stalemate.

blocks.question: Select all legal ways to escape a check:
options: Ignore it and play another move
blocks.explanation: You must respond to check by moving the king, capturing the attacker, or blocking (for line-piece checks). Ignoring check is illegal. Resigning ends the game but is not a way to 'escape' check within the rules.

blocks.question: What symbol is used in algebraic notation to indicate checkmate?
blocks.explanation: The '#' symbol denotes checkmate. '+' denotes check. '++' is sometimes used for double check, but '#' is the standard checkmate symbol.
